title: Kidneys Kept Super-Cold for Days Work Perfectly in Pigs!
summary: What if we could keep a donated kidney fresh for days instead of hours? Right now, doctors have only about 24 hours to get a kidney from a donor to a patient. After that, it can go bad. But scientists just did something amazing: they kept pig kidneys super-cold—way below freezing—for three whole days, and then put them back into pigs. And guess what? The kidneys worked great! Normally, if you freeze an organ, ice forms inside and destroys it. But a team led by Matthew Powell-Palm at Texas A&M University built a special device. It's a sealed chamber that keeps the kidney under pressure while cooling it to -4°C (25°F). That's colder than your freezer, but no ice forms! They used a liquid that's already used to preserve organs. Powell-Palm calls it 'low-tech high science.' After 24, 48, or even 72 hours, they transplanted the kidneys back into pigs. The kidneys started making urine right away and worked normally within about 10 days. That's faster than kidneys kept on ice for 24 hours! Over 30 days, the pigs grew, and their super-cooled kidneys grew with them—almost doubling in size. One pig was watched for 200 days, and its kidney still looked healthy. In the US, over 104,000 people are waiting for a kidney. Every day, 17 people die waiting. This discovery could mean more kidneys can be saved and used, giving hope to thousands. The team is super excited, and they're working to make this ready for humans someday.
why_it_matters: This could mean that one day, if someone in your family or community needs a kidney, there will be a better chance to get one in time.

background_read: Kidneys are two bean-shaped organs that clean your blood by removing waste and extra water to make urine. When someone’s kidneys stop working, they need a new one from a donor to survive.

Matthew Powell-Palm is a scientist at Texas A&M University, a large school in the United States. He calls this discovery ‘low-tech high science’ because it uses simple physics to solve a giant medical puzzle.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists led by Matthew Powell-Palm at Texas A&M University.
WHAT: Kept pig kidneys super-cold (-4°C, 25°F) without freezing for up to 3 days, then successfully transplanted them.
WHERE: In a laboratory at Texas A&M University (the pigs were cared for there).
WHY: To make more donated kidneys usable and save the many people who die waiting for a transplant.

perspectives.description: Thousands of people waiting for a kidney may have a new reason to hope, because this method could let many more organs be saved and used.
The experiment was only in pigs, so we still need to prove it works safely in humans—and building the special high-pressure devices for hospitals might be expensive.
